name: Painite
physical: Said to bring a warm, sturdy feeling
Crystal healers link it with endurance
summary: Painite is one of the rarest minerals ever found, a red-brown Burmese gem once counted in handfuls and linked in crystal lore with endurance and vitality.
intro: Painite is a calcium zirconium aluminium borate that appears in shades of ruddy orange, red-brown and deep garnet-red, usually as hexagonal crystals with a rough, glassy surface. For decades it held the title of rarest mineral on Earth: by 2004 only two crystals were known, and only a few dozen faceted stones had been cut. New finds in Myanmar's Namya area in the 2000s raised the number, but painite remains an extraordinary collector's piece. Some crystals are opaque and best displayed rough, while rare transparent ones are faceted into small, warm-coloured gems with a distinct red glow, particularly bright under certain lights.
history: Painite was found in the 1950s by the British gemologist Arthur Charles Davy Pain in Mogok, Burma, who gave a small brownish crystal to the British Museum. It was formally described as a new mineral in 1957 and named in his honour. For many years only a couple of specimens existed, kept in museums. Greater discoveries arrived in 2001 and in subsequent years with the opening of the Namya mine in Kachin State, bringing hundreds of crystals to market. Even so, painite is still scarcer than most gemstones, and many examples contain minute black inclusions or have unusual colour.
meaning: In crystal tradition painite is a stone of perseverance, rarity and endurance. Its earthy red-brown colours link it with the root and sacral chakras, and practitioners say it supports stamina, patience and courage in long undertakings. Because it was once nearly lost to science, many see it as a symbol of resilience and of hidden things coming to light. Few people will ever hold one, so it is often used as a theme for meditation on unexpected value. Physically it is traditionally associated with stamina and warmth, as a symbolic companion rather than a treatment, and it is best considered a stone of the collector's imagination.
howToUse: If you own raw painite, keep it as a display piece on a shelf or altar to remind you of resilience and the value of persistence. Touch the stone gently at the start of a long project and breathe slowly to focus your will. If you do not have painite, red-brown stones such as garnet, red jasper or smoky quartz can stand in for similar themes. Meditate on the story of its discovery and what rare qualities you hold. Use it in a grid with hematite and carnelian for endurance work.
care: Painite is hard and stable, so a gentle rinse with lukewarm water and a soft brush is safe. Avoid ultrasonic cleaners if the crystal has fractures or inclusions. Cleanse energetically with smoke, sound, moonlight or sunlight. Because pieces are rare and valuable, store each in a padded box, separate from harder gems. Handle rough crystals with care, as they may have sharp edges and delicate zones. Keep documentation and certificates with each stone.
identify: Painite is distinctive in chemistry and structure, so laboratory testing is the only reliable way to identify it. It often resembles garnet, tourmaline, zircon, ruby and red-brown glass. Raw crystals are hexagonal, with a vitreous to resinous lustre and ruddy brown colour. Because the price is very high, insist on a certificate from a recognised gemmological laboratory that confirms painite and its origin. Be extremely wary of any inexpensive stone sold under this name.

faq.q: Is painite really the rarest mineral?
faq.a: For decades it held that title, with only two known crystals until the early 2000s. New discoveries in Myanmar have increased the number, but painite remains far scarcer than any common gemstone.
British gemologist Arthur Charles Davy Pain found a small crystal in Mogok, Burma, in the 1950s. The mineral was named painite in his honour after the British Museum confirmed it was new.

faq.q: What does painite mean in crystal tradition?
faq.a: It is a symbol of endurance, resilience and hidden value. Linked to the root and sacral chakras, it is used as a meditation theme for perseverance, though real specimens are rarely owned.
